metadata.title: Welcome and starter
metadata.summary: Meet the unit, then choose one emerging technology example.

content.text: Welcome
This unit is Exploring New and Emerging Digital Technologies (M/618/3683). Across the year you will outline technologies, then explain how people and organisations use them.

Digital technology changes quickly. Businesses that notice new tools early can improve service, cut cost or stay safe. This lesson is formative practice for LO1 / AC 1.1. It is not Gateway assignment evidence.

content.title: By the end of this lesson
content.text: Define digital technology; tell current from emerging; outline mobile, intelligent computing, IoT and cloud; and spot simple business uses.

Misconception: learners often treat any new phone as emerging. Extension: ask for one sector where a current tool is still emerging. Discussion: why must businesses adapt? Differentiation: pair write the starter before sharing.
Starter

content.prompt: Which of these is an example of an emerging digital technology?

options.label: A desktop PC used for word processing in most offices
Quantum computing still in limited research and early commercial trials
A wired classroom projector that has been in schools for years
A paper timetable on a noticeboard

feedback.correct: Quantum computing is still developing and is not widely adopted, so it is emerging.
feedback.incorrect: Emerging technology is still developing or not yet widely used. A common office PC or projector is current.

metadata.title: What is digital technology?
metadata.summary: Outline devices, software, networks and data, then match each description to a technology.

content.text: What is digital technology?
Digital technology uses electronic devices and software to create, store, share or process data.
Devices are the hardware, such as phones, sensors and servers. Software is the programs and apps that tell hardware what to do.
Networks connect devices so they can share data. Data is the information those systems collect, such as a location, a payment or a temperature reading.
Match the description

content.prompt: Match each description to the technology. Descriptions are listed in mixed order.

items.label: Physical objects that collect or share data over a network, often with little manual input
items.text: Physical objects that collect or share data over a network, often with little manual input

items.label: Software that finds patterns, makes predictions or generates content
items.text: Software that finds patterns, makes predictions or generates content

items.label: Computing resources such as storage or software delivered over the internet
items.text: Computing resources such as storage or software delivered over the internet

items.label: Portable devices and apps used away from a desk, including phones and tablets
items.text: Portable devices and apps used away from a desk, including phones and tablets

feedback.correct: Each description now matches the right technology.
feedback.incorrect: Read each description again. Look for device, network, software pattern or internet-delivered resource.

metadata.title: Current versus emerging
metadata.summary: Explain the difference, then sort examples.

content.text: Current vs emerging technologies
Current technology is already in common use. Most people or organisations in that setting already rely on it.
Emerging technology is still developing, is costly, or is not yet widely adopted. The same product can be current in one sector and emerging in another.
Example: contactless payment is current in many UK shops. A consumer brain-computer headset is still emerging.
Ask: would most people in this setting already use it this year?

content.prompt: Sort each example as current or emerging for a typical UK college learner in 2026.

items.label: Desktop PC
items.text: Desktop PC

items.label: Smartphone
items.text: Smartphone

items.label: Driverless cars as everyday personal transport
items.text: Driverless cars as everyday personal transport

items.label: Quantum computing
items.text: Quantum computing

items.label: Cloud storage such as OneDrive or Google Drive
items.text: Cloud storage such as OneDrive or Google Drive

items.label: An AI assistant built into everyday software
items.text: An AI assistant built into everyday software

items.label: A wearable health monitor used by some people but not yet by most
items.text: A wearable health monitor used by some people but not yet by most

feedback.correct: Current tools are already common. Emerging tools are still limited, costly or not widely used.
feedback.incorrect: A smartphone and cloud storage are already common. Driverless cars and quantum computing are not everyday tools yet.

metadata.title: Mobile technology
metadata.summary: Outline mobile uses, then select the mobile examples.

content.text: Mobile technology
Mobile technology is computing you can carry. Smartphones and tablets run apps for messaging, maps, learning and work.
Mobile payments let people tap a phone or watch to pay. GPS gives location for maps, deliveries and safety.
Mobile banking lets customers check balances, pay bills and approve logins without a branch visit.
Select the mobile examples

content.prompt: Choose Mobile for every example that is mobile technology. Choose Not mobile for the distractors.

items.label: A banking app on a smartphone
items.text: A banking app on a smartphone

items.label: A tablet used to sign for a parcel
items.text: A tablet used to sign for a parcel

items.label: Tapping a phone to pay for lunch
items.text: Tapping a phone to pay for lunch

items.label: Using GPS to find a college campus
items.text: Using GPS to find a college campus

items.label: A desktop tower that never leaves the office
items.text: A desktop tower that never leaves the office

items.label: A printed paper form in a filing cabinet
items.text: A printed paper form in a filing cabinet

feedback.correct: Mobile examples are portable devices, apps, payments or GPS. A desktop or paper form is not.
feedback.incorrect: Look for phones, tablets, apps, tap-to-pay or GPS. A desktop PC and paper records are not mobile technology.

metadata.title: Intelligent computing
metadata.summary: Outline AI, machine learning, automation and robotics, then judge five statements.

content.text: Intelligent computing
Intelligent computing is software and machines that can perform tasks that used to need human judgement, such as spotting a pattern or choosing a next step.
Artificial intelligence (AI) is the broad idea. Machine learning is a common method: the system improves by training on examples rather than only following fixed rules.
Automation runs a process with little human input, such as sorting invoices. Robotics uses machines that move or handle objects, sometimes with AI to decide what to do next.
True or false

content.prompt: Machine learning is one way a system can improve by training on examples.

feedback.correct: Machine learning trains on data so the system can improve without rewriting every rule by hand.
feedback.incorrect: Machine learning trains on data so the system can improve without rewriting every rule by hand.

content.prompt: Every robot in a factory must also be an internet-connected wearable.

feedback.correct: Robotics is about machines that move or handle objects. A factory robot is not a wearable, and it may or may not be connected to the internet.
feedback.incorrect: Robotics is about machines that move or handle objects. A factory robot is not a wearable, and it may or may not be connected to the internet.

content.prompt: Automation can reduce repetitive data-entry work.

feedback.correct: Automation is often used for repeated processes such as copying invoice data.
feedback.incorrect: Automation is often used for repeated processes such as copying invoice data.

content.prompt: AI can only be used for generating images, never for spotting fraud.

feedback.correct: Banks already use AI-style pattern detection to flag unusual payments.
feedback.incorrect: Banks already use AI-style pattern detection to flag unusual payments.

content.prompt: Intelligent computing always replaces every human job on day one.

feedback.correct: These tools usually support or change tasks. They do not instantly remove every role.
feedback.incorrect: These tools usually support or change tasks. They do not instantly remove every role.

metadata.title: Internet of Things
metadata.summary: Outline connected devices, then group consumer and business examples.

content.text: Internet of Things
The Internet of Things (IoT) is a network of physical devices that collect or share data, often with little manual input.
Smart homes use connected lights, speakers and thermostats. Wearables such as a fitness watch are IoT when they send health or activity data.
Industrial IoT uses sensors and machines in warehouses and factories to track stock, temperature or equipment.
Consumer or business IoT?

content.prompt: Group each example as consumer IoT or business IoT.

items.label: Smart watch
items.text: Smart watch

items.label: Smart thermostat in a house
items.text: Smart thermostat in a house

items.label: Warehouse sensors
items.text: Warehouse sensors

items.label: Smart factory robot
items.text: Smart factory robot

items.label: Connected car used by a family
items.text: Connected car used by a family

items.label: RFID scanner in a stock room
items.text: RFID scanner in a stock room

feedback.correct: Consumer examples are used by people at home or on the move. Business examples support stock, factories or scanning.
feedback.incorrect: A watch, home thermostat or family car is consumer. Warehouse sensors, factory robots and RFID scanners are business.

metadata.title: Cloud technology
metadata.summary: Outline SaaS, IaaS and PaaS, then complete each sentence.

content.text: Cloud technology
Cloud technology delivers computing over the internet instead of only from one local device. Users can often scale up or down as they need.
SaaS is software you use in a browser or app, such as email. IaaS rents infrastructure such as virtual machines and storage. PaaS gives a ready place to build and run applications.

content.title: Keep it simple
content.text: Ask who manages the application. If the provider runs the app for you, it is usually SaaS.
Complete the sentences

content.prompt: Google Docs is an example of ______.

feedback.correct: The provider runs the document app. You just use it, which is SaaS.
feedback.incorrect: Google Docs is software delivered as a service, not a sensor network or a ledger.

content.prompt: Renting virtual machines and then installing your own software is ______.

feedback.correct: You manage the machines. The cloud supplies the infrastructure, which is IaaS.
feedback.incorrect: IaaS is infrastructure: virtual machines, storage and networks.

content.prompt: A hosted environment for building and running an app is ______.

feedback.correct: PaaS supplies the platform so developers can build and run software.
feedback.incorrect: PaaS is a platform for building apps, not a tag, map or local PC.

content.prompt: College email in a browser is closest to ______.

feedback.correct: The provider runs the email application. Learners just use it.
feedback.incorrect: Browser email is software as a service.

content.prompt: Which statement best outlines cloud technology?

options.label: Computing resources delivered over the internet
A USB stick that never connects to a network
A calculator with no data connection

feedback.correct: Cloud services are delivered over the internet and can usually scale.
feedback.incorrect: Cloud is internet-delivered computing, not an offline object.

content.prompt: A team that only wants extra disk space during exam week is mainly buying ______.

feedback.correct: Extra virtual disks are infrastructure capacity.
feedback.incorrect: Storage capacity is IaaS, not a wearable or a payment tap.

Retail, banking, entertainment and healthcare all use digital tools, but not always the same ones. Choose the best fit for each organisation in this lesson.

items.label: Classroom Wi-Fi

items.text: A personal holographic display that few shops sell

feedback.incorrect: IoT devices collect or share data, often automatically, over a network.

content.prompt: Which option is intelligent computing rather than a simple calculator?

Adding two numbers with a basic handheld calculator

content.prompt: SaaS is best outlined as ______.

content.prompt: Match the remaining pair.

items.label: Soil sensors sending moisture readings from a field

metadata.title: Welcome to Week 2
metadata.summary: Set the focus for AC1.1: outline IoT, connected devices, RFID, NFC and wearables.

content.text: Welcome to Week 2
This week you outline Internet of Things (IoT), connected devices, RFID, NFC and wearables (AC1.1).
By the end, define each technology, give an example, and note one benefit and one risk.

content.prompt: Which best describes the Internet of Things (IoT)?

options.label: A single desktop PC with no network link
Physical devices that collect or share data over a network
Printed barcodes that never use radio
A paper rota on a noticeboard

feedback.correct: IoT is a network of physical devices that collect or share data, often automatically.
feedback.incorrect: IoT is a network of physical devices that collect or share data, often automatically.

metadata.title: IoT and connected devices
metadata.summary: Outline what IoT is and what makes a device 'connected'.

content.text: IoT and connected devices
IoT devices sense, act or share data with little manual input. A connected device can send or receive data over a network (Wi-Fi, mobile, Bluetooth or similar).
Examples: smart thermostat, warehouse temperature sensor, connected street light, hospital infusion pump that reports status.

content.prompt: A device is 'connected' mainly when it can:

options.label: Only store data offline with no network path
Send or receive data over a network

feedback.correct: Connected devices exchange data over a network.
feedback.incorrect: Connected devices exchange data over a network.

content.prompt: Which is the best IoT example?

options.label: A paper clipboard in a storeroom
Soil moisture sensors uploading readings to a farm dashboard
An unplugged desk lamp with no radio

feedback.correct: Sensors sharing field data are a classic IoT use.
feedback.incorrect: Sensors sharing field data are a classic IoT use.

metadata.title: Consumer, industrial and healthcare IoT
metadata.summary: Classify IoT examples by sector.

content.text: Consumer, industrial and healthcare IoT
Consumer IoT is for homes and personal use. Industrial IoT supports factories, farms and logistics. Healthcare IoT supports patients and clinical monitoring.

content.prompt: Match each example to the sector.

items.text: Smart home heating controlled from a phone
Factory machine vibration sensors for maintenance
Wearable heart-rate monitor used in a clinic trial
Fridge camera helping a household reorder milk
Cold-store sensors in a warehouse
Connected drip pump reporting dose alerts

feedback.correct: Those matches look right.
feedback.incorrect: Check the definition and try again.

metadata.title: RFID principles
metadata.summary: Outline how RFID tags and readers identify items.

content.text: RFID
RFID uses radio tags and readers to identify items. Readers can often scan tags without lining every item up under a camera, which helps stock and asset tracking.
Typical uses: clothing tags in retail, pallet tags in warehouses, library books, tool tracking on a site.

content.prompt: RFID is most useful when an organisation needs to:

options.label: Identify tagged items at short distance without lining each one under a camera
Replace all radio with paper only
Project a hologram in a classroom
Run a spreadsheet with no tags

feedback.correct: RFID readers identify tagged items at short range, including when items are not lined up one by one.
feedback.incorrect: RFID readers identify tagged items at short range, including when items are not lined up one by one.

content.prompt: Give one business use of RFID.
content.guidance: Mention tagged items and tracking or scanning. Write at least 100 characters. Paste is disabled.

metadata.title: NFC principles
metadata.summary: Outline NFC as very short-range radio for secure taps.

content.text: NFC
NFC (Near Field Communication) is very short-range radio, usually centimetres. It suits short taps such as contactless payment, door badges and ticket gates.

content.prompt: NFC is designed to work over:

options.label: Very short range (about a few centimetres)

feedback.correct: NFC is for close taps over a few centimetres.
feedback.incorrect: NFC is for close taps over a few centimetres.

content.prompt: Which is the best NFC example?

options.label: Tapping a phone on a till to pay
A printed poster with no electronics
A long-range warehouse aisle scan of 200 tagged boxes at once

feedback.correct: Contactless payment taps use NFC.
feedback.incorrect: Contactless payment taps use NFC.

metadata.title: RFID versus NFC
metadata.summary: Compare RFID and NFC by range and typical use.

content.text: RFID versus NFC
Both use radio, but NFC is for very close taps. RFID often supports stock/asset tagging where a reader covers a short area and many tags.

content.prompt: Classify each statement.

items.text: Best for scanning many tagged boxes in a stock room
Best for a phone tap at a payment terminal
Often used on clothing security tags
Usually limited to a few centimetres

feedback.correct: Those matches look right.
feedback.incorrect: Check the definition and try again.

metadata.title: Wearable technologies
metadata.summary: Outline wearables and how they link to IoT.

content.text: Wearables
Wearables are devices worn on the body: fitness watches, smart badges, medical patches. Many are IoT devices when they upload activity or health data.

content.prompt: Which is a wearable?

options.label: A rack server in a data centre

feedback.correct: Wearables are worn on the body.
feedback.incorrect: Wearables are worn on the body.

content.prompt: A wearable becomes an IoT example mainly when it:

options.label: Never leaves airplane mode and never shares data
Shares sensor data over a network to an app or service

feedback.correct: Shared sensor data over a network makes it an IoT wearable.
feedback.incorrect: Shared sensor data over a network makes it an IoT wearable.

metadata.title: Smart homes, cities and healthcare settings
metadata.summary: Match connected examples to smart home, smart city or healthcare.

content.text: Smart homes, cities and healthcare
The same IoT idea appears in homes, cities and healthcare, with different goals: comfort, public services, or patient safety.

content.prompt: Match each example.

items.text: Connected thermostat learning household routines
Street lights that dim when roads are empty
Remote monitoring of a patient's oxygen levels
Smart door lock for a flat
Traffic sensors feeding a live congestion map
Hospital bed sensor alerting when a patient leaves the bed

feedback.correct: Those matches look right.
feedback.incorrect: Check the definition and try again.

metadata.title: Benefits, risks and security
metadata.summary: Check benefits of connected tech and key security risks.

content.text: Benefits, risks and security
Benefits include automation, better decisions from live data, and convenience. Risks include hacking, outages, cost, and poor configuration.

content.prompt: A clear benefit of industrial IoT sensors is that they can:

options.label: Remove the need for any safety rules
Provide live data to spot faults earlier

feedback.correct: Live sensor data helps spot faults and improve decisions.
feedback.incorrect: Live sensor data helps spot faults and improve decisions.

content.prompt: A key security risk for always-on IoT devices is:

options.label: Weak passwords or unpatched firmware can be exploited

feedback.correct: Weak credentials and missing updates are common IoT security risks.
feedback.incorrect: Weak credentials and missing updates are common IoT security risks.

metadata.title: Privacy and case study thinking
metadata.summary: Consider privacy implications and outline a short case study.

content.text: Privacy and real-world cases
Wearables and healthcare IoT often handle sensitive data. Organisations need consent, clear purpose, access control and secure storage.

content.prompt: Main privacy risk if a fitness wearable leaks heart-rate data?

options.label: Private health details exposed without consent

feedback.correct: Leaked health data is a privacy and consent issue.
feedback.incorrect: Leaked health data is a privacy and consent issue.

content.prompt: Outline one real-world case: name the technology (IoT, RFID, NFC or wearable), who uses it, and one risk to manage.
content.guidance: Write 2-4 short sentences (at least 350 characters). Paste is disabled. This is practice only.

metadata.title: Emerging trends
metadata.summary: Spot sensible near-term trends for connected devices.

content.text: Emerging trends
Trends include more sensors in cities, tighter security expectations, edge processing on devices, and wearables used in workplace health programmes.

content.prompt: Which statement is a realistic emerging trend?

options.label: All IoT devices will stop using networks
More organisations expect stronger IoT security and updates
RFID will only work on the Moon
NFC will replace all long-distance radio

feedback.correct: Security and update expectations for IoT are rising.
feedback.incorrect: Security and update expectations for IoT are rising.

metadata.title: Welcome to Week 3
metadata.summary: Retrieve where data lives, then set the focus for cloud service models (AC1.1).

content.text: Welcome to Week 3
This week you outline cloud technology and distinguish SaaS, IaaS, PaaS and DaaS (AC1.1).
By the end, define cloud computing, match everyday services to a model, and write a short cloud profile.

content.prompt: A fitness watch from Week 2 uploads heart-rate readings to an app account. Where is that health data mainly stored for later viewing?

options.label: Only inside the watch with no other copy
Often on remote servers accessed over the internet (the cloud), as well as on the device
Only on a printed paper chart
Only in a classroom USB stick that never connects

feedback.correct: Connected devices often keep a local copy and also send data to cloud services so it can be viewed later on other devices.
feedback.incorrect: Connected devices often keep a local copy and also send data to cloud services so it can be viewed later on other devices.

metadata.title: What is cloud technology?
metadata.summary: Outline cloud computing as internet-delivered resources that can scale.

content.text: What is cloud technology?
Cloud technology delivers computing resources over the internet instead of only from one local device or a single on-site server. Users can often scale up or down and pay for what they use.
Examples include web email, online file storage, rented virtual machines, hosted app platforms and remote desktops.

content.prompt: Which statement best outlines cloud technology?

options.label: Computing resources delivered over the internet, often scaled as needed
A single USB stick that never connects to a network
Only paper filing cabinets in one office
A projector that cannot store or share files

feedback.correct: Cloud means resources are delivered over the internet and can usually grow or shrink with demand.
feedback.incorrect: Cloud means resources are delivered over the internet and can usually grow or shrink with demand.

content.prompt: Saving a document only on the hard drive of one classroom PC (never uploaded) is mainly an example of:

feedback.correct: If the file stays only on that PC, it is local storage, not cloud storage.
feedback.incorrect: If the file stays only on that PC, it is local storage, not cloud storage.

metadata.title: Local storage versus cloud
metadata.summary: Classify examples as local storage or cloud storage.

content.text: Local storage versus cloud
Local storage keeps files on a device you control in the room. Cloud storage keeps files on remote servers you reach over the internet.

content.prompt: Classify each example.

items.text: A homework file saved only on a laptop hard drive
Photos backed up to Google Drive or OneDrive
Music stored only on a phone with airplane mode and no sync
College email messages held on the provider's mail servers
A spreadsheet on a USB stick that never uploads
Shared team files in a browser-based document suite

feedback.correct: Those matches look right.
feedback.incorrect: Check the definition and try again.

metadata.title: SaaS
metadata.summary: Outline Software as a Service with familiar examples.

content.text: SaaS (Software as a Service)
SaaS is software you use through a browser or app. The provider runs and updates the application. You mainly manage your account, content and access rights.

content.prompt: Using college email in a browser is closest to:

options.label: Only local storage with no provider

feedback.correct: The email application is provided and managed for you. That is SaaS.
feedback.incorrect: The email application is provided and managed for you. That is SaaS.

content.prompt: In SaaS, who usually installs security updates for the application itself?

options.label: Every learner must install the app updates on school servers

feedback.correct: The provider maintains the SaaS application. Customers focus on using it and managing their data access.
feedback.incorrect: The provider maintains the SaaS application. Customers focus on using it and managing their data access.

metadata.title: IaaS
metadata.summary: Outline Infrastructure as a Service: rented virtual machines, storage and networks.

content.text: IaaS (Infrastructure as a Service)
IaaS rents infrastructure such as virtual machines, storage and networks. The customer installs and manages operating systems and software. The provider manages the physical data centre hardware.

content.prompt: An IT team rents virtual servers and then installs its own operating systems and apps. This is mainly:

feedback.correct: Renting virtual servers and managing the software stack yourself is IaaS.
feedback.incorrect: Renting virtual servers and managing the software stack yourself is IaaS.

content.prompt: A college rents extra virtual disks during exam week, then scales down afterwards. This mainly shows:

options.label: That IaaS-style resources can scale with demand
That only SaaS can use disks
That local USB sticks are required

feedback.correct: Scaling storage up and down is a common cloud benefit, often via infrastructure services.
feedback.incorrect: Scaling storage up and down is a common cloud benefit, often via infrastructure services.

metadata.title: PaaS
metadata.summary: Outline Platform as a Service for building and running applications.

content.text: PaaS (Platform as a Service)
PaaS gives a ready environment to build, test and run applications. The provider manages the platform. Developers focus on their app code rather than buying and patching every server.

content.prompt: Developers deploy an app into a hosted build-and-run environment. This is mainly:

feedback.correct: A hosted environment for building and running apps is PaaS.
feedback.incorrect: A hosted environment for building and running apps is PaaS.

content.prompt: Compared with IaaS, PaaS usually means the customer:

options.label: Must build the physical data centre
Manages less of the underlying servers and focuses more on the application

feedback.correct: PaaS reduces how much infrastructure the customer manages so they can focus on the application.
feedback.incorrect: PaaS reduces how much infrastructure the customer manages so they can focus on the application.

metadata.title: DaaS
metadata.summary: Outline Desktop as a Service: a desktop session delivered over the network.

content.text: DaaS (Desktop as a Service)
DaaS delivers a desktop environment over the network. The user works on a remote desktop rather than relying only on software installed on one local PC.

content.prompt: Staff log in to a Windows desktop that runs in the cloud. This is mainly:

feedback.correct: A full desktop session delivered remotely is Desktop as a Service (DaaS).
feedback.incorrect: A full desktop session delivered remotely is Desktop as a Service (DaaS).

content.prompt: DaaS is best outlined as:

options.label: A desktop environment delivered over the network
A physical tower PC that cannot be accessed remotely

feedback.correct: DaaS provides a desktop session remotely over the network.
feedback.incorrect: DaaS provides a desktop session remotely over the network.

metadata.title: Match services to cloud models
metadata.summary: Classify everyday services as SaaS, IaaS, PaaS or DaaS.

content.text: Match services to cloud models
Ask what you are buying: a ready app (SaaS), raw infrastructure (IaaS), an app platform (PaaS), or a remote desktop (DaaS).

content.prompt: Classify each example.

items.text: Learners write documents in a browser-based office suite
An IT team rents virtual servers and installs its own software stack
Developers deploy an app into a hosted build-and-run environment
Staff log in to a Windows desktop that runs in the cloud
A class uses a hosted quiz tool with no local install
A college rents extra virtual disks during exam week
College email opened in a browser
A remote desktop used from a thin client in a library

feedback.correct: Those matches look right.
feedback.incorrect: Check the definition and try again.

metadata.title: Who manages what?
metadata.summary: Classify responsibilities as mainly customer or mainly provider.

content.text: Who manages what?
In cloud models, some jobs stay with the customer and some stay with the provider. The split changes across SaaS, IaaS, PaaS and DaaS.

content.prompt: For a typical SaaS email service, classify each responsibility.

items.text: Choosing strong passwords and careful sharing settings
Patching the email application on the provider servers
Deciding which classmates may edit a shared folder
Keeping the data centre power and cooling running
Writing the message content of your own emails
Updating the SaaS product features for all tenants

feedback.correct: Those matches look right.
feedback.incorrect: Check the definition and try again.

metadata.title: Which model fits?
metadata.summary: Choose the best cloud model for each organisational scenario.

content.text: Which model fits?
Read each scenario and pick the model that best matches what the organisation is buying.

content.prompt: A small charity wants staff to use email and shared docs without running its own mail servers. Best fit:

feedback.correct: Ready-to-use apps with little server management point to SaaS.
feedback.incorrect: Ready-to-use apps with little server management point to SaaS.

content.prompt: A college IT team wants full control of operating systems on rented virtual machines. Best fit:

feedback.correct: Control of OS and software on rented machines is IaaS.
feedback.incorrect: Control of OS and software on rented machines is IaaS.

content.prompt: A start-up wants developers to deploy code quickly without building servers from scratch. Best fit:

feedback.correct: A ready build-and-run platform for developers is PaaS.
feedback.incorrect: A ready build-and-run platform for developers is PaaS.

content.prompt: A business wants staff to open the same managed Windows desktop from home or campus. Best fit:

feedback.correct: A managed desktop delivered over the network is DaaS.
feedback.incorrect: A managed desktop delivered over the network is DaaS.

metadata.title: Cloud benefits and dependencies
metadata.summary: Check benefits of cloud use and key dependencies or risks.

content.text: Benefits, dependencies and risks
Cloud can reduce on-site equipment needs and support scaling. It can also create dependency on a provider, internet access and good account security.

content.prompt: A clear benefit of cloud for many organisations is:

options.label: They never need internet access again
They can often scale capacity without buying new on-site hardware every time
Providers delete all customer data daily by default with no backup option

feedback.correct: Scaling without constantly buying new local hardware is a common cloud benefit.
feedback.incorrect: Scaling without constantly buying new local hardware is a common cloud benefit.

content.prompt: A key dependency or risk of heavy cloud use is:

options.label: No one ever needs a password
Service outages or lock-in can affect work if the provider or internet link fails

feedback.correct: Organisations depend on connectivity and the provider. Outages and lock-in are real risks to manage.
feedback.incorrect: Organisations depend on connectivity and the provider. Outages and lock-in are real risks to manage.

content.prompt: Give one benefit of using cloud technology and one dependency or risk an organisation should manage.
content.guidance: Write at least 300 characters. Mention one benefit and one dependency or risk. Paste is disabled.

metadata.title: Organisational cloud example
metadata.summary: Outline one organisation and how it uses a cloud model.

content.text: Organisational cloud example
Organisations use cloud services for email, storage, development platforms, virtual machines and remote desktops.

content.prompt: Name one organisation (real or realistic). State which cloud model it uses in your example and what the service is for.
content.guidance: Write at least 300 characters. Name the organisation, the model (SaaS, IaaS, PaaS or DaaS), and the purpose. Paste is disabled.

metadata.title: Extension: SaaS or IaaS for a small business?
metadata.summary: Explain why a small business might choose SaaS rather than IaaS.

content.text: Extension: SaaS or IaaS?
Small organisations often prefer ready apps over managing servers. Larger IT teams may want IaaS for control.

content.prompt: A three-person charity with no IT team needs email and shared files quickly. The stronger first choice is usually:

options.label: Building a private data centre first

feedback.correct: With little IT capacity, SaaS reduces the need to run and patch your own servers.
feedback.incorrect: With little IT capacity, SaaS reduces the need to run and patch your own servers.

content.prompt: In your own words, explain why a small business might choose SaaS rather than IaaS.
content.guidance: Write at least 250 characters. Link your reason to skills, time or cost. Paste is disabled.

metadata.summary: Produce a short cloud profile naming the service, model and organisation context.

content.text: Cloud technology profile
Independent task: build a short profile you could reuse when outlining technologies for AC1.1 practice. This is formative, not Gateway assignment evidence.

content.prompt: Write a cloud profile: name one cloud service, state whether it is closest to SaaS, IaaS, PaaS or DaaS, say who uses it, give one benefit, and give one dependency or risk.
content.guidance: Cover service, model, who uses it, one benefit and one dependency or risk. Write at least 500 characters. Paste is disabled.

Cloud = no network; Local = always remote servers
